Question: Which statement is not accurate?

Options:
A. A species can react as an electrophile if it contains an atom (other than hydrogen) with an incomplete valence octet
B. A species can react as an electrophile, even if it has one or more unshared electron pairs
C. Any species bearing a lone pair can normally react as a nucleophile

Thought: I need to analyze each statement and determine which one is not accurate regarding electrophiles and nucleophiles in chemistry.

A. A species can react as an electrophile if it contains an atom (other than hydrogen) with an incomplete valence octet.
This is accurate. Electrophiles are electron-loving species that accept electrons, and atoms with incomplete octets are electron-deficient, making them electrophilic.

B. A species can react as an electrophile, even if it has one or more unshared electron pairs.
This is accurate. For example, boron trifluoride (BF₃) has an incomplete octet on boron, making it electrophilic, even though the fluorine atoms have unshared electron pairs.

C. Any species bearing a lone pair can normally react as a nucleophile.
This is accurate. Nucleophiles are electron-rich species that donate electrons, and lone pairs are available for donation in chemical reactions.

D. It is not necessary for a nucleophile to have an unshared electron pair.
This statement is NOT accurate. By definition, nucleophiles donate electron pairs in reactions. While some nucleophiles can use π-bonds as electron sources, they still need electron pairs (either as lone pairs or in π-bonds) to act as nucleophiles. A species without any electron pairs to donate cannot function as a nucleophile.
Final Answer: [ANSWER]D[/ANSWER]
